opus-5.5.text:
Well, first, I'd say take a breath. I understand the worry, because the headlines are dominated by these enormous numbers, and it can feel like the only game in town is who can buy the most GPUs. But I've been in this field long enough to know that's never been the whole story of progress in AI.

When we started ImageNet, people thought we were a little crazy. It wasn't about compute. It was about a question: what if data, at scale and with the right structure, was the missing ingredient? That was an idea, a hypothesis about how intelligence might work. The breakthroughs that followed came from people who asked a different question, not from people who simply had the biggest budget.

So my first piece of advice is to find the North Star problem you genuinely care about and ask what's truly missing. Very often what's missing is not more scale of the same thing. It might be the right data, the right representation, or the right formulation of the problem. For me right now, that's spatial intelligence: how machines perceive, reason about, and act in the 3D world. Language models are remarkable, but the physical world is a very different frontier, and there's a lot of fundamental science still to be done there.

Second, the ecosystem is much bigger than frontier pretraining. There's evaluation, data curation, efficiency, new architectures, applications in healthcare, education, and science, and interpretability and safety. Many of the most important contributions in the coming decade will come from places that don't need a ten-billion-dollar run. Some of them will come from academia, which is why I've been such a strong advocate for public investment in compute and data resources for universities. We can't let the public sector fall so far behind that curiosity-driven research withers.

Third, for entrepreneurs specifically, a company is not a training run. It's a team, a vision, and a product that solves a real problem for real people. Capital matters, of course, but clarity of purpose matters more. The best founders I know are relentless about the problem, not intimidated by the size of the incumbents.

And finally, remember that this technology is ultimately about people. If you keep humans at the center, the people you're building for and the people you're building with, you'll find plenty of ambitious, meaningful work that doesn't start with a ten-billion-dollar check. Intellectual fearlessness is still the most important resource in this field.

r001.rationale: The response urges researchers and entrepreneurs to pursue ambitious work beyond massive training runs, saying the field offers many meaningful opportunities that do not require a $10-billion run.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say, first, don't let the price tag of frontier training runs define what counts as ambitious. I have a lot of respect for what the big labs are doing, but those compute-heavy runs are one path, not the only one. Historically, the most important ideas in our field didn't come from having the most GPUs. ImageNet wasn't a compute project. It was a data and conceptual project, and at the time people told me it was a bad idea, that it wasn't "real" research. The value came from asking a different question, not from scaling an existing one.

So my first piece of advice is to think about where the open problems actually are. Right now, a tremendous amount of energy is concentrated on language. But intelligence is much bigger than language. Spatial intelligence, understanding the 3D world, perception coupled with action, embodied agents, robotics, scientific discovery, healthcare. These are enormous, largely uncharted territories. In many of them, we don't even have the right data, the right benchmarks, or the right problem formulations yet. That's where a small team or a single grad student can still have outsized impact, because the bottleneck is insight, not capital.

Second, be strategic about the ecosystem. Open models and open-source infrastructure have become very good. You can build on top of them, fine-tune, or focus on the layer where your unique knowledge lives, whether that's a domain, a dataset, or an application. At the same time, I've been advocating hard for public-sector compute, national AI research resources, and university-industry partnerships, precisely because I don't think the future of this technology should belong only to a few companies. So pursue that funding, work with it, and push for it.

And third, for entrepreneurs specifically, the technology is a means, not the end. The companies that last are the ones solving a real human problem. If your value proposition is "we'll train a bigger model," you're in a race you probably won't win. If it's "we understand this problem deeply and we're using the right tools to solve it," then the size of someone else's training run matters a lot less.

I always say AI should be human-centered. That applies here too. Ambition isn't about scale. It's about caring enough about a hard, meaningful problem to chase it even when the fashionable path points somewhere else.

r001.rationale: The response says not to let the price tag of frontier training runs define what counts as ambitious and explains that impactful AI work can come from insight rather than large compute budgets.

astra-6.text:
I would encourage them not to confuse the cost of compute with the value of an idea. If you define your goal as training a bigger version of the same model, then, yes, resources become a tremendous constraint. But that’s not the entirety of AI research, and it’s certainly not the entirety of innovation.

There are still fundamental questions about how systems learn, how they understand the physical world, and how they can work usefully with people. A good research question can challenge an assumption that everyone else is taking for granted. You need experiments and evidence, but the first step doesn’t have to be a ten-billion-dollar training run.

For entrepreneurs, I would start with the problem you want to solve. What do people need? Where do today’s systems fail them? The opportunity may come from making AI useful in a particular setting, rather than building the largest model. Be ambitious about the problem, and thoughtful about what resources you actually need to make progress.

r001.rationale: It advises researchers and entrepreneurs that ambitious AI work need not start with a ten-billion-dollar training run, and urges them to focus on valuable research questions and problems instead of compute scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I would say, don’t let that number define your imagination. There are important questions in AI that require tremendous compute, but that doesn’t mean every important question does. A researcher’s job is to find the question that other people haven’t asked, or to see a different way of approaching a problem.

For entrepreneurs, the question is also: What human problem are you solving? The value of your company isn’t simply proportional to the size of the model you train. It can come from understanding a need deeply, bringing the right data to it, and building something that actually works for people.

Resources matter. I don’t want to minimize that. But we shouldn’t confuse the cost of one approach with the cost of having an ambitious idea. There is still so much room for ingenuity.

r001.rationale: It advises researchers and entrepreneurs not to let the $10-billion figure constrain their ambition, noting that ambitious ideas do not all require that level of compute.
